lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's early, unmistakable declaration that he loves her as well as her poetry.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth's wondering whether their near-miss meeting had really happened.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Robert turns their first contact from 'honour of acquaintance' into friendship and a spring meeting.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: A vivid spring promise that he will surely see her.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Elizabeth's private joke redefining spring in her own 'style'.

lines.text: But if my truest heart's wishes avail, as they have hitherto done, you shall laugh at East winds yet, as I do!
lines.note: Robert's callback to Elizabeth's east-wind complaint, promising she will laugh at east winds.

lines.text: You and I seem to meet in a mild contrarious harmony ... as in the 'si no, si no' of an Italian duet.
lines.note: Elizabeth's private image of their 'mild contrarious harmony' like an Italian duet.

lines.text: And I, too, love to have few friends, and to live alone, and to see you from week to week.
lines.note: Robert's quiet statement of wanting few friends and seeing her week to week.

lines.text: And you do like the 'Duchess,' as much as you have got of it? that delights me, too--for every reason.
lines.note: Robert's delight that Elizabeth likes the 'Duchess'.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's declaration that his whole life is wound around her.

lines.text: God bless and strengthen you, my ever dearest dearest—I will not trust myself to speak of my feelings for you—worship well belongs to such fortitude.
lines.note: A farewell blessing as the journey to Italy nears.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's last-moment sense that she will have him only to love her.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Elizabeth's explicit question of whether this is her last letter.

lines.text: Do you pray for me to-night, Robert?
lines.note: Elizabeth's final request that he pray for her.
